info.text: Quiz: 20 questions (multiple choice, code tracing, drag and drop).

questiontext.text: Which statement describes the difference between set and multiset correctly?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Both containers keep their elements sorted. The only difference here is duplicates: set ignores a second copy of a value, while multiset stores it.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: A set rejects a value that is already stored; a multiset keeps every copy
A set is sorted; a multiset is never sorted
A set stores only numbers; a multiset stores any type
A set is faster to read by index; a multiset has no index

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
set<int> s;
for (int x : {5, 3, 5, 1, 3}) {
    s.insert(x);
}
cout << s.size() << ":";
for (int x : s) {
    cout << " " << x;
}
cout << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Only the first copy of 5 and of 3 is kept, so three distinct values remain. Walking over a set always gives them from smallest to largest.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: What does s.find(x) return when x is not in the set s?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. find returns an iterator. When the value is missing the iterator is end(), a position after the last element that must never be read.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
set<int> s = {10, 20, 30, 40};
cout << *s.lower_bound(20) << " " << *s.upper_bound(20) << " " << *s.lower_bound(25) << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. lower_bound(20) is the first element that is greater than or equal to 20, so it is 20 itself. upper_bound(20) is the first element that is strictly greater, which is 30. And lower_bound(25) skips 20 and lands on 30.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Arrange the lines so the program prints 0 (the value 5 is added and then removed before it is counted).

Drag the lines into the order the computer runs them.

order the lines
 1  [[1]]
 2  [[2]]
 3  [[3]]
 4  [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. A set must exist before you use it, the value must be inserted before it can be erased, and the question comes last. If erase ran before insert, the program would print 1.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
set<int> s;
s.insert(5);
s.erase(5);
cout << s.count(5) << endl;

questiontext.text:
What does this code print?

main.cpp
multiset<int> m = {3, 3, 3, 1};
m.erase(3);
cout << m.count(3) << " " << m.size() << endl;

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Erasing by value removes every copy of that value from a multiset. All three 3s disappear and only the 1 remains, so the count is 0 and the size is 1.

name.text: Q07 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct word into the gap so that the program prints 15 (the first element strictly greater than 8).

main.cpp
set<int> s = {4, 8, 15};
auto it = s.[[1]](8);
cout << *it << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. upper_bound(8) returns the first element greater than 8, which is 15. lower_bound(8) and find(8) would both point to 8 itself.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
set<int> s = {4, 8, 15};
auto it = s.upper_bound(8);
cout << *it << endl;

questiontext.text:
Match each set command with what it does.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

s.insert(x)  →  [[1]]

s.erase(x)  →  [[2]]

s.count(x)  →  [[3]]

s.find(x)  →  [[4]]

*s.rbegin()  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. These five operations cover most of what you do with a set. Notice that the last one reads through a reverse iterator.

The correct answer:

  • s.insert(x) → Adds x unless it is already there
  • s.erase(x) → Removes the value x if it exists
  • s.count(x) → Gives 1 if x exists and 0 if it does not
  • s.find(x) → Gives an iterator to x, or end() when it is missing
  • *s.rbegin() → The largest element

questiontext.text:
Sort each statement: does it compile for set<int> s = {1, 2, 3};?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

s.insert(4);  →  [[1]]

s[0] = 5;  →  [[2]]

*s.begin() = 9;  →  [[2]]

s.erase(2);  →  [[1]]

cout << *s.rbegin();  →  [[1]]

s.push_back(4);  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. A set has no indices and no push_back, and its elements are read-only because their position depends on their value. These statements were all tested with a real compiler.

The correct answer:

Compiles: s.insert(4);, s.erase(2);, cout << *s.rbegin();
Does not compile: s[0] = 5;, *s.begin() = 9;, s.push_back(4);

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
multiset<int> m = {2, 2, 5};
m.erase(m.find(2));
cout << m.count(2) << " " << m.size() << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Erasing through an iterator removes exactly one copy. One 2 remains, and the multiset holds {2, 5}, so the size is 2.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: What is the running time of insert, erase and find on a set with n elements?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A set is built on a balanced search tree, so each operation walks down a path whose length grows like the logarithm of n.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: What is the shortest correct way to count the distinct values of a vector v?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Building a set from the vector throws the duplicates away, so its size is the number of distinct values.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
set<int> s = {10, 20, 30};
auto it = s.lower_bound(25);
--it;
cout << *it << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. lower_bound(25) points to 30. Stepping back one position reaches 20, which is the largest element smaller than 25.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: Why is s.lower_bound(x) better than lower_bound(s.begin(), s.end(), x) for a set?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Set iterators cannot jump, so the generic algorithm advances one element at a time and costs O(n). The member function descends the tree directly.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: The member function uses the tree and stays O(log n); the generic one walks element by element
The generic one does not compile on sets
The member function returns a number instead of an iterator
There is no difference at all

name.text: Q16 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Complete the declaration so that the numbers print in descending order (321).

Drag the correct pieces into the gaps.

main.cpp
set<int, [[1]]<int>> s = {3, 1, 2};
for (int x : s) {
    cout << x;
}
cout << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The second template argument decides the ordering. greater<int> puts larger values first, while less<int> is the default ascending order.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
set<int, greater<int>> s = {3, 1, 2};
for (int x : s) {
    cout << x;
}
cout << endl;

questiontext.text:
Match each container with its main property.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

set  →  [[1]]

multiset  →  [[2]]

unordered_set  →  [[3]]

vector  →  [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Choosing the right container is half of the solution: ask whether you need order, duplicates, or the fastest possible lookup.

The correct answer:

  • set → Sorted, no duplicates
  • multiset → Sorted, duplicates allowed
  • unordered_set → No guaranteed order, fast on average
  • vector → Indexed, duplicates allowed, not sorted by itself

questiontext.text:
Sort each container: does it remove duplicate values when you insert them?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

set<int>  →  [[1]]

multiset<int>  →  [[2]]

vector<int>  →  [[2]]

unordered_set<int>  →  [[1]]

map<int, int> (its keys)  →  [[1]]

multimap<int, int> (its keys)  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The set family and the keys of a map are unique. The multi versions and the vector keep every copy.

The correct answer:

Removes duplicates: set<int>, unordered_set<int>, map<int, int> (its keys)
Keeps duplicates: multiset<int>, vector<int>, multimap<int, int> (its keys)

questiontext.text: When would you choose unordered_set instead of set?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. unordered_set is usually faster for plain membership tests, but it has no order, so it cannot answer "smallest" or "closest" questions.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: When you only ask "is it there?" and do not need order or lower_bound
When you need the smallest element quickly
When you need to walk over the values in ascending order
When you need to find the closest value above x
